The flood story belongs to every continent and is older than any of the rivers it names; the species remembers being small and afraid of the rising water, and tells the story to its children to make sure we do not forget.
A myth is the slow agreement between a culture's deepest fear and its most patient hope, and the gods are the masks the agreement wears so the children can hear it.
The gods of a mythology, properly understood, are not external beings but internal organs of the culture that imagined them; to study a mythology is to read a society's anatomy.
The trickster, the hero, and the wise woman are the three sentences the species has not stopped saying in any language; the rest of mythology is footnotes.
